Land and Sea Use Planning. By 2040, at least 24% of terrestrial and inland water, and 16% of marine and coastal areas accomplished biodiversity inclusive spatial analysis and planning

Land and Sea Use Planning. By 2040, at least 24% of terrestrial and inland water, and 16% of marine and coastal areas accomplished biodiversity inclusive spatial analysis and planning Actions necessary to achieve the national target: Formulation and adoption of management Plans for Protected Areas and OECMs with geo-spatial plans on land use, vulnerability and risks, tenurial instruments Geo-spatial Plans: Develop geo-spatial plans that overlay land use, vulnerability, risks, and tenurial instruments. Relevant stakeholders include DENR, specifically the Land Management Bureau (LMB), in collaboration with LGUs, NEDA, and other relevant government agencies. Conduct of Management Effectiveness Assessment using the Management Effectiveness Tracking Tool (METT) or MEAT in Protected Areas and OECMs Development of a policy that will install ARA compliance Integration of Spatial Planning within Protected Areas (PAs) Management Plans: Ensure that all protected areas under the National Integrated Protected Areas System (NIPAS/eNIPAS) and Other Effective Area-based Conservation Measures (OECM) Registry have integrated spatial planning in their conservation and management plans. Relevant stakeholders include the Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR), specifically the Biodiversity Management Bureau (BMB), in collaboration with the Protected Area Management Boards (PAMBs), LGUs, NCIP and the Indigenous People (for the ICCAs), other relevant stakeholders for the OECMs. Expansion of OECM Registry Participation: Increase the participation of the different government agencies, LGUs, private sector, civil society, academia, and other sectors in the OECM Registry. Relevant stakeholders include the DENR-BMB, in coordination with various government agencies, LGUs, and stakeholders. Inclusive Planning Process: Ensure the participation of women and men, including Indigenous Peoples (IP) and non-IP communities, in the planning process, maintaining at least a 60-40 ratio. Relevant stakeholders include DENR-BMB, National Commission on Indigenous Peoples (NCIP), National Economic and Development Authority (NEDA), and LGUs. Allocate funds to implement the approved management plans. These actions, when implemented in coordination and collaboration with national government agencies and other stakeholders, will enable the Philippines to achieve its target of effectively planning and managing all areas to reduce biodiversity loss by 2040.
Ecosystem Restoration

Ecosystem Restoration. By 2040, at least 30% of degraded terrestrial (upland and lowland), inland water, coastal, and marine ecosystems restored/rehabilitated, resulting to enhanced biodiversity, ecosystem functions, ecological integrity, and connectivity

Ecosystem Restoration. By 2040, at least 30% of degraded terrestrial (upland and lowland), inland water, coastal, and marine ecosystems restored/rehabilitated, resulting to enhanced biodiversity, ecosystem functions, ecological integrity, and connectivity To achieve the target of restoring 30% of all degraded ecosystems by 2040 in the Philippines, the following actions have been identified: Identification of Degraded Areas: Conduct dialogues to achieve a shared understanding of biologically degraded areas and agree on action steps for restoration. Conduct comprehensive assessments to identify ecologically and biologically degraded terrestrial, inland water, coastal, and marine ecosystems. The relevant stakeholders include the Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR), National Mapping and Resource Information Authority (NAMRIA), scientific institutions, local government units (LGUs), indigenous communities. These would require environmental assessments, biodiversity surveys, and remote sensing data among others. Development of Restoration/Rehabilitation Plans: Detailed restoration and rehabilitation plans for selected degraded sites should be prepared, incorporating scientific assessments, community input, and stakeholder consultations. The relevant stakeholders include the DENR, LGUs, Department of Agriculture (DA), Department of Science and Technology (DOST), academic institutions, NGOs, indigenous communities. Critical information from the academe (ecosystem restoration methodologies and guidelines), some scientific research and stakeholder (community consultations) is needed. Restoration or rehabilitation plans would include NAPERSEP, NGP, Implementation of Restoration Activities: The execution of the approved restoration plans (i.e. reforestation, habitat restoration, soil conservation, waterway rehabilitation, and marine ecosystem restoration) will follow with the collaboration of relevant stakeholders like the DENR, LGUs, DA, Department of Agrarian Reform (DAR), Department of Interior and Local Government (DILG), private sector partners, NGOs, communities. At this point implementation guidelines, project management plans, and standardized monitoring protocols are essential. Capacity Building and Training: Training and capacity-building programs to equip stakeholders with the necessary skills and knowledge for effective ecosystem restoration and management should be given. Important stakeholders include the DENR, LGUs, academic institutions, NGOs, indigenous communities, and the local community. The need for the development of training modules and the conduct of workshops would ensue (Target 20). Monitoring and Evaluation: Similar to the other targets with actions or indicators identified
Protect and Conserve Land and Sea

Protect and Conserve Land and Sea. By 2040, at least 24% of terrestrial and inland water, and 16% of coastal and marine areas are effectively conserved and managed (especially areas of particular importance for biodiversity and ecosystem functions and services).

Protect and Conserve Land and Sea. By 2040, at least 24% of terrestrial and inland water, and 16% of coastal and marine areas are effectively conserved and managed (especially areas of particular importance for biodiversity and ecosystem functions and services). The main document here would be the OECM list being drafted by the DENR which would consolidate in the list the different areas being protected by different agencies and people. This includes: LGU – protected areas; KBAs, reference ecosystems of the mining areas, biodiversity corridors wherein priority species move or inhabit. The ancestral domains of the IPs although part of the protected area (protection by the IPs) may not be included in the OECM but will be included in the tabulation of the protected areas. There are more areas which have been identified but these are being validated and some need to undergo stakeholders consultation or agreements. To support the achievement of the target to conserve 30% of land and sea by 2040 in the Philippines, several actions involving various stakeholders should be taken. Identification and Designation of New Protected Areas: Identification of potential OECMs, numerical targets for 30x30, keystone/threatened species Involvement of government agencies/ LGUs/ private sector/ civil society/ academe/ other sectors on the establishment/designation/management of OECMs and updating the OECM Registry Designate new protected areas under the National Integrated Protected Areas System (NIPAS) Act and Expanded NIPAS Act. Conduct comprehensive assessments to identify ecologically significant areas deserving protection (these would include locally managed MPAs, KBAs, ICCAs, and OECMs). Engage with indigenous peoples and local communities to recognize and integrate their territories into protected area management plans (ancestral domains). The ancestral domains are large tracts of land and marine areas (ancestral domain waters) which could be a huge contribution to the 30% target. Tabulate the areas of protection under several levels of protection to ensure the 30% protection of land and sea. Development of Ecologically Sound and Inclusive Conservation and Management Plans: Formulation and adoption of management Plans for Protected Areas and OECMs with geo-spatial plans on land use, vulnerability and risks, tenurial instruments Adoption of Management Plans for Protected Areas and OECMs with Geo-spatial plans on land use, vulnerability and risks, tenurial instruments Allocate adequate funding for the implementation of these plans, including resources for biodiversity monitoring, enforcement, and community engagement. Establishment of Functioning Management Bodies: Assess the status of each governance body viz target sites Develop
Active Management of Species and Genetic Diversity

Active Management of Species and Genetic Diversity. By 2040, governance and management regimes are improved for threatened species; native crops, livestocks, wild relatives; and their genetic resources

Active Management of Species and Genetic Diversity. By 2040, governance and management regimes are improved for threatened species; native crops, livestocks, wild relatives; and their genetic resources Actions which will be taken to achieve the national target includes: Assessment and Monitoring of Threatened Species (for different taxa) included in the national list using the Red List Index (agreed upon by experts). The assessment of the species should be a continuing activity for both terrestrial (with freshwater) and marine species. This includes the creation of maps: to include distribution and routes (of migratory species) to establish locations. These will facilitate local participation in conservation and monitoring. Establishment of native species seed banks and nurseries to conserve genetic diversity and ensure the availability of native plant species for restoration and conservation efforts in several areas in the country. This is linked to the restoration of degraded habitats as per Target 2. Development and Implementation of Conservation Plans for priority threatened wildlife species. This includes habitat protection, population management, and local stakeholder engagement (most specially for continuous species monitoring). Linked to Targets 1, 2 and 3. Improvement of Wild Populations of Economically Important Species via habitat restoration (Target 2), sustainable harvesting practices (Target 5), and fisheries management (Target 3, 5). Establishment and Maintenance of Wildlife Rescue Centers both terrestrial and aquatic/marine wildlife rescue centers to provide care, rehabilitation, and release of injured or displaced wildlife. Conservation of Migratory Species and Wetlands by protecting routes of migratory species in inland and coastal wetlands sites through the establishment of a network of protected areas or biodiversity corridors, habitat restoration, and community-based conservation initiatives (Targets 2 and 3). Protection of native livestock by continuing and supporting efforts of academe and other research agencies instituting genetic conservation programs, sustainable breeding practices. Another would be supporting traditional livestock farming communities (e.g. IPs – Target 22). These actions would contribute to the achievement of other specific targets of the KMGBF and the PBSAP. Relevant agencies are DENR, DA and NGOs.
Harvest, Trade, and Use of Wild Species

Harvest, Trade, and Use of Wild Species. By 2040, wildlife species harvested from the wild are traded within the allowed limits and conditions set by RA 9147 (Wildlife Act), By 2030, the Harvest Control Rules and Reference Points for capture fisheries under RA 10654 and its IRR are in place

Harvest, Trade, and Use of Wild Species. By 2040, wildlife species harvested from the wild are traded within the allowed limits and conditions set by RA 9147 (Wildlife Act), By 2030, the Harvest Control Rules and Reference Points for capture fisheries under RA 10654 and its IRR are in place Several policy measures and actions will be done to achieve the Philippine target: Fortified with full time staff, budget and authority, the National Convergence Initiative (NCI) which will ensure harmonization and mainstreaming biodiversity in all relevant priority programs and projects that utilize/ impact on natural resources/ecosystems should be fully implemented. (NEDA) Development of science-based allowable harvest limits and harvesting guidelines for priority species in terrestrial, coastal, and marine ecosystems, established in accordance with the provisions set forth in Republic Act No. 9147 (Wildlife Act) and its implementing rules and regulations (Joint DENR-DA-PCSD AO 2004-01). Addition of economic incentives and policies to encourage stakeholders to shift towards less destructive means of harvesting wild species. This may include tax incentives, subsidies, and market-based mechanisms to promote sustainable harvesting practices (Target 18). Implement measures to reduce by-catch of vulnerable and target species through the use of selective fishing gear and practices. This would include the strengthened efforts to combat illegal trade of wildlife through increased monitoring, surveillance, and law enforcement activities. Strengthen wildlife regulation and enforcement activities by enhancing coordination among agencies, increasing patrols and inspections, and increasing penalties for wildlife-related offenses (Target 3, NCI). Capacitate an appropriate number of enforcers to perform their duties effectively in regulating wildlife trade which includes training, providing equipment, and support to enforcement personnel (Target 3, 4, 20). Implement components of the Zoonoses program, including the Philippine Surveillance System, to monitor and address zoonotic diseases transmitted from wildlife to humans. Adopt and implement the One Health program to promote interdisciplinary collaboration and holistic approaches to health management, including planetary health considerations. Issue seed collection guidelines for native and endemic species to ensure sustainable harvesting practices. Baseline inventories of native Non-Timber Forest Products (NTFPs) to assess their status and inform sustainable management strategies will be conducted. Develop audience-specific (harvesters, traders, buyers) educational materials and require them to undertake sustained CEPA on comprehensive issues emanating from illegal use/trade (Target 20)
Invasive Alien Species
Invasive Alien Species. By 2040, the spread of invasive alien species (IAS) reduced by 50% in priority sites.

Invasive Alien Species. By 2040, the spread of invasive alien species (IAS) reduced by 50% in priority sites. The NISSAP was crafted and adopted jointly by the Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR and the Department of Agriculture (DA) (Joint DENR-DA AO 2020-02) in pursuit of the objectives of: the Wildlife Resources Conservation and Protection Act (Republic Act No. 9147), the Expanded National Integrated Protected Areas System (NIPAS) Act (Republic Act No. 11038), the Plant Quarantine Law (Presidential Decree No. 1433), the Amended Philippine Fisheries Code of 1998 (Republic Act No. 10654), and the Philippine commitments under the Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD), and to address the threats of invasive alien species (IAS) to Philippine biodiversity, economy and social welfare. These are taken from the joint administrative order: There are nine (9) strategic goals towards a holistic, collaborative and multi-sectoral approach in managing the risks of IAS: (1) leadership and coordination; (2) prevention; (3) early detection and rapid response; (4) control and management; (5) restoration; (6) research and information management; (7) education and public awareness; (8) international cooperation; and (9) training needs. Each of the nine strategic goals provide its guiding principles, objectives, implementing guidelines and planned actions spanning three timelines - short term (2020-2021), medium term (2022-2023) and long term (2024-2030). The joint resolution stipulates that: the Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR) through the Biodiversity Management Bureau (BMB), Ecosystems Research and Development Bureau (ERDB), Forest Management Bureau (FMB), and Environmental Management Bureau (EMB); and the Department of Agriculture (DA) through the Bureau of Plant Industry (BPI), Bureau of Fisheries and Aquatic Resources (BFAR), and Bureau of Animal Industry (BAI) shall disseminate the NISSAP, undertake capacity building for field offices and other relevant agencies, coordinate the conduct of surveys and researches, undertake public awareness campaigns, and develop specific policy guidelines to ensure efficient and effective implementation of the NISSAP by all concerned. In addition, the DENR, through the BMB and the DA through its Policy Research Service shall facilitate the creation of the inter-agency coordinating body for IAS. Further, both the DENR and DA, in collaboration with other concerned agencies and stakeholders are hereby authorized to coordinate the implementation and mainstreaming of the NISSAP with the plans and programs
Reduce Pollution
Reduce Pollution. By 2040, reduce nutrient run-off and pesticide-related impacts on non-target organisms and ecosystem by at least 50%

Reduce Pollution. By 2040, reduce nutrient run-off and pesticide-related impacts on non-target organisms and ecosystem by at least 50% Actions for this target should be under the jurisdiction of several government agencies. The DA and the DENR should have a joint resolution to collaborate and achieve the national target regarding agricultural waste. The DENR with the DILG, leagues of municipalities and cities should also have a resolution for addressing household waste. The DENR (EMB) addresses industrial waste. Invest in training programs and capacity- building initiatives for agricultural stakeholders to promote awareness and understanding of sustainable agricultural practices and pollution reduction measures (DA). Support research initiatives focused on developing and promoting biodiversity-friendly and toxic-free agricultural inputs and practices. Foster collaboration between research institutions, agricultural universities, and the private sector to innovate solutions (DA). Strengthen extension services to provide technical assistance and guidance to farmers on adopting sustainable farming methods, including organic farming, integrated pest management, and soil conservation practices (DA). Provide financial incentives, subsidies, and grants to farmers who transition to sustainable agricultural practices and invest in pollution reduction measures. Establish financing mechanisms to support the adoption of environmentally friendly technologies and inputs (Target 19) (DA). Enact and enforce regulations that promote sustainable agriculture and pollution reduction, including laws banning or restricting the use of harmful chemicals and inorganic fertilizers. Ensure compliance with environmental standards and monitor agricultural activities for pollution prevention (DA). Preparation of information on baselines of pesticide and other pollutants (classified according to types, degree and extent of impacts, users, etc.). Implementation of phased-out or reduced use programs for harmful chemical, inorganic fertilizers, pesticides and other pollutants. Monitoring of water quality from 2023 levels. Facilitate market access for producers of biodiversity-friendly and organic agricultural products by providing market information, certification support, and access to fair trade networks. Foster collaboration between government agencies, civil society organizations, academic institutions, and the private sector to coordinate efforts and share best practices in pollution reduction and sustainable agriculture.
Minimize the Impact of Climate Change

Minimize the Impact of Climate Change. By 2040, the impacts of climate change are minimized and disaster risks reduced through Nature-based solutions and/or Ecosystem-based approaches, and relevant indigenous knowledge systems and practices

Minimize the Impact of Climate Change. By 2040, the impacts of climate change are minimized and disaster risks reduced through Nature-based solutions and/or Ecosystem-based approaches, and relevant indigenous knowledge systems and practices To achieve Target 8, a series of strategic actions are needed. Increase the Number of Climate-proofed Protected Area Management Plans Prepare baseline information (with vulnerability assessment report) per target against threats/climate perils (historical and/or probabilistic). Conduct vulnerability and risk assessments in terrestrial, coastal, marine and other natural ecosystems Identify the most significant climate change threats to each protected area, including risks from increased temperatures, sea-level rise, extreme weather events, and ocean acidification. Mainstream Nature-based Solutions (NBS) Across Sectoral Plans Prepare NBS prescriptions in vulnerable areas. Design nature-based solutions tailored to each protected area's unique ecosystems and threats, focusing on restoring and conserving natural habitats to enhance resilience against climate change. Climate- proof and incorporate NBS prescriptions of Protected Area Management Plan, LLCAP, NCCAP/NAP, NDRMM,CLUP(CDRA), Watershed Management Plan, among others adopted and implemented (with vulnerability & risk assessments; Nature-based solutions Programs, Activities, and Projects (NBS PAPs); climate insurance, Automated Weather Station (AWS), etc) Enhance Ecosystem Resilience: Strengthen the resilience of ecosystems within protected areas through reforestation, mangrove restoration, and the protection of coral reefs to reduce the impact of storms, flooding, and other disasters. Adopt and Enforce Stricter Zoning and Land-Use Policies: Prevent development and activities that could increase vulnerability to climate impacts, such as deforestation, unsustainable tourism, and construction in high-risk areas. Increase coastline planted to mangroves Legislate/pass national policy on greenbelts Integrate NBS into National and Local Development Plans: Work with relevant government agencies to ensure that nature-based solutions are incorporated into broader national and local development, agriculture, fisheries, and urban planning policies. Promote Cross- sectoral Collaboration: Foster partnerships between government agencies, non-governmental organizations, the private sector, and local communities to implement and scale up nature-based solutions. Sustainable Use and Benefit-Sharing. By 2040, wildlife species harvested from the wild are traded within the allowed limits and conditions set by RA 9147 (Wildlife Act), By 2030, the Harvest Control Rules and Reference Points for capture fisheries under RA 10654 and its IRR are in place The measures and actions are not going to be achieved without the actions of various stakeholders from the NGAs (DENR, DA, DILG, NCIP, NEDA, DILG (LGUs), DOST, CHED (SUCs)) (and their line agencies), NGOs, ACB, etc. To achieve the indicators listed for KMGBF Target 9 in the Philippines, several activities need to be implemented (in collaborations with other relevant agencies/stakeholders) to provide information for each indicator. Implement actions to minimize impacts of unsustainable practices on wildlife : Strict enforcement of laws and policies against illegal trade of wildlife Conduct a review of existing wildlife protection laws and regulations to identify gaps and areas for improvement. Develop and implement new policies and regulations targeting hunting, poaching, and illegal wildlife trade, with a focus on protecting vulnerable and migratory species. Strengthen law enforcement agencies and capacity to combat wildlife crime through training, equipment provision, and collaboration with other agencies and stakeholders. Establish partnerships with international organizations and neighboring countries to address transboundary issues related to wildlife conservation and illegal trade. Issuance of wildlife permits Compliance monitoring of permit holders Determination of annual quota for wild collection (with conditions to address sustainability issues). Document by-catch of vulnerable and target species (DENR, DA: BFAR): Reporting and active monitoring of by-catch of vulnerable and target species Conduct comprehensive surveys and assessments of harvesting, hunting and fishing activities in different terrestrial, marine and freshwater ecosystems to quantify by-catch of vulnerable and target species. Monitoring of wild populations of economically important terrestrial and aquatic species Develop monitoring programs and protocols to record and document by-catch data, including species composition, quantities, and harvesting, hunting and fishing methods used. Engage gatherers, hunters and fishers and local and fishing communities in participatory monitoring and data collection efforts to enhance accuracy and coverage. Analyze by-catch data to identify trends, hotspots, and potential mitigation measures to reduce impacts on vulnerable species. Sustainable Management of Agriculture, Aquaculture, and Forestry

Sustainable Management of Agriculture, Aquaculture, and Forestry. By 2040, agriculture, fisheries, aquaculture, and forestry production levels are sustainably managed, resilience improved and long-term productivity maintained 70% upland agricultural landscapes (areas) within KBAs and watershed forest reserves implement biodiversity-friendly agricultural practices. 50% of all rice and corn areas deemed suitable for commodity systems, lowland modality of BDFAP are under that modality as defined by the NAFMIP (Note: Target for lowland and upland)

Sustainable Management of Agriculture, Aquaculture, and Forestry. By 2040, agriculture, fisheries, aquaculture, and forestry production levels are sustainably managed, resilience improved and long-term productivity maintained 70% upland agricultural landscapes (areas) within KBAs and watershed forest reserves implement biodiversity-friendly agricultural practices. 50% of all rice and corn areas deemed suitable for commodity systems, lowland modality of BDFAP are under that modality as defined by the NAFMIP (Note: Target for lowland and upland) Promotion and Adoption of Biodiversity-Friendly Agricultural Practices (DA-ATI, BFAR; DENR FMB): Identification of production zones in each target site and promotion of adoption of climate smart, sustainable, and biodiversity-friendly forestry, agriculture, fishery and aquatic production practices. Develop and implement training programs and extension services to educate farmers about the benefits and techniques of biodiversity-friendly practices such as organic farming, Sustainable Land Management (SLM) technologies, and Integrated Pest Management (IPM). Provide financial incentives and technical support to farmers who adopt biodiversity-friendly practices, including subsidies for organic certification and access to alternative pest management solutions. Establish demonstration farms and model villages to showcase successful implementation of biodiversity-friendly practices and their positive impacts on productivity and sustainability. Provide material, financial and technical support to willing SLM adopters especially during the transition to BDFAPs wherein expected incomes may be reduced Collaborate with agricultural cooperatives, non- governmental organizations (NGOs), and private sector partners to disseminate information and facilitate knowledge exchange among farmers. Establishing the practice of using the supply chain and value chain principles in local commerce including preparation of habitat and production plan Creation of measures of gauging the improvement in local trade and economy due to good farming and conservation practices. *consult with NEDA Expansion of Sustainable Forest Management (DENR FMB, Target 3): Conduct comprehensive assessments of forest resources to identify priority areas for sustainable forest management, focusing on increasing the coverage of production forests. Develop and implement forest management plans that integrate biodiversity conservation, ecosystem services, and community livelihoods, with active involvement of local stakeholders. Strengthen law enforcement and monitoring mechanisms to prevent illegal logging, forest encroachment, and unsustainable harvesting practices. Promote community-based forest management approaches, recognizing the rights and traditional knowledge of indigenous peoples and local communities. Regulation of Air, Hazards and Extreme Events. By 2040, resilience and stability of ecosystems and habitats are maintained and enhanced, especially those in vulnerable areas/situations and high exposure areas, and those communities most dependent on biodiversity.

Regulation of Air, Hazards and Extreme Events. By 2040, resilience and stability of ecosystems and habitats are maintained and enhanced, especially those in vulnerable areas/situations and high exposure areas, and those communities most dependent on biodiversity. To achieve Target 11 the Philippines needs to take a series of strategic actions aligned with identified indicators. Below is a plan of action for each identified indicator: Conduct Post Disaster Needs Assessments (PDNA) in Priority Protected Areas (PAs) and Other Effective Area-Based Conservation Measures (OECMs) Conduct of Post Disaster Needs Assessments (PDNA) / blue and green assessment (BGA) in priority PAs after every disaster Develop and Implement a Standardized PDNA Protocol: Tailor this protocol for ecosystems and biodiversity, focusing on assessing the impact of disasters on the living conditions and livelihood of IPLC women and men living within PAs and OECMs and ecosystem services and biodiversity in priority PAs and OECMs. Train Teams in PDNA: Build capacity among local government units (LGUs), environmental NGOs, and community groups to conduct PDNAs effectively following disasters. Perform Resource Valuation of Ecosystem Services and Species in Priority PAs Preparation of baseline of Ecosystem Goods and Services (EGS) for each target site through National Capital Accounting (NCA) Preparation of baseline on benefits (each target site) of EGS to local trade and economy, including downstream communities through resource valuation Investment planning (each target site) to generate funds and other resources to restore and protect the sources of EGS. Developing agreements (each target site) for PES to generate additional funds to conserve the sources of EGS and designing fund reflows (each target site) to conserve the sources (habitats) of EGS Establish a Comprehensive Ecosystem Valuation Framework: Develop guidelines for evaluating the economic, social, and cultural value of ecosystem services and species within protected areas. Conduct Valuations Regularly: Ensure these valuations are performed periodically to monitor changes and inform management decisions and policy development. Conduct Resource/Ecosystem Valuation of Priority Species and Ecosystem Services (Targets 1, 2, 3, 4, 5) Prioritize Key Species and Ecosystem Services: Identify which species and services are most critical for valuation efforts, focusing on those with significant impacts on human well-being. Utilize a Mix of Valuation Methods: Apply both quantitative and qualitative methods to capture the full range of ecosystem services values. Increase Access to Green and Blue Spaces
Increase Access to Green and Blue Spaces. By 2040, urban green and blue spaces in all cities accessible to the public increased

Increase Access to Green and Blue Spaces. By 2040, urban green and blue spaces in all cities accessible to the public increased To achieve the target of enhancing green spaces and urban planning for human well-being and biodiversity, as outlined by Target 12 and adopted by the Philippines various actions have been identified to attain the target: Promotion of City Biodiversity Index (CBI) Adoption: Develop guidelines and provide technical assistance to cities on the adoption and implementation of the City Biodiversity Index (CBI) (Target 20). Conduct training workshops and awareness campaigns to educate local government officials and planners about the importance of biodiversity-inclusive urban planning (Target 20). Expansion of Green and Blue Spaces: Inventory of Green Spaces in Priority Cities Establishment/ Designation of green and blue spaces Identify potential sites for the establishment or expansion of green and blue spaces in urban and densely populated areas. Collaborate with local government units (LGUs), private landowners, and community stakeholders to acquire land and develop green and blue infrastructure projects that can be made accessible to local residents and visitors. Prioritize the conservation and restoration of native biodiversity in green and blue spaces to enhance ecological connectivity and integrity (Targets 2 and 3). Support for LGUs in Achieving Seal of Good Local Governance (SGLG) Indicators: Conduct of Urban Biodiversity Assessment and Profiling Urban Biodiversity Management Planning Urban Biodiversity Management Plan Implementation Provide technical assistance and capacity building to LGUs to help them comply with SGLG indicators related to urban green and blue spaces (Target 20). Develop resource materials and best practice guidelines to assist LGUs in planning, implementing, and monitoring green and blue infrastructure projects (Target 20). Development and Implementation of Policy on Blue and Green Infrastructure : Adoption and Implementation of Blue and green infrastructure/Sustainable Infrastructure Framework & Roadmap with policy instrument approved Collaboration among national government agencies (DENR, Department of the Interior and Local Government (DILG) and other relevant agencies to develop a policy on blue and green infrastructure/sustainable infrastructure framework & roadmap. Advocate for the adoption and implementation of the policy at the national and local levels, ensuring alignment with existing urban planning and development frameworks. Fair and Equitable Sharing of Benefits from Genetic Resources

Fair and Equitable Sharing of Benefits from Genetic Resources. By 2040, there is a significant increase of the benefit shared, with providers and rights holders in accordance with applicable international ABS instruments

Fair and Equitable Sharing of Benefits from Genetic Resources. By 2040, there is a significant increase of the benefit shared, with providers and rights holders in accordance with applicable international ABS instruments To support the Philippine government in achieving the target of increasing the sharing of benefits from genetic resources, digital sequence information, and traditional knowledge, several actions can be taken. Development and Implementation of Access and Benefit Sharing (ABS) Guidelines: Develop comprehensive ABS guidelines to regulate access to genetic resources and ensure fair and equitable benefit-sharing arrangements. Establish procedures for obtaining permits and conducting negotiations with stakeholders, including indigenous communities and local governments. Capacity Building Programs (Target 20): Conduct capacity-building programs to enhance the understanding of ABS principles and procedures among relevant stakeholders, including government officials, researchers, indigenous peoples, and local communities. Provide training on negotiation skills, conflict resolution, and legal aspects of ABS agreements. Legislative and Policy Reforms: Review and amend existing laws and policies to strengthen the legal framework for ABS, ensuring alignment with international agreements and best practices. Develop new legislation or regulations to address gaps in ABS governance and enforcement. Establishment of Multi-Lateral Systems: DENR can work with relevant government agencies, such as the Department of Agriculture (DA), to establish a multi-lateral system under the International Treaty on Plant Genetic Resources for Food and Agriculture (ITPGRFA). Facilitate collaboration with other countries and international organizations to promote the exchange of genetic resources and ensure fair and equitable benefit-sharing. Creation of Registries and Seed Banks: Establish centralized registries or databases of native species and genetic resources to facilitate access and tracking (Targets 4 and 21). Support the establishment and maintenance of seed banks and germplasm repositories to conserve and preserve genetic diversity (Target 4). Implementation of DNA Barcoding Programs: Institutionalize DNA barcoding programs to enable the identification and authentication of genetic resources. Collaborate with research institutions and academic partners to conduct DNA barcoding studies and build capacity in this area. Establishment of Philippine Access and Benefit Sharing (PH ABS) Clearing House: Work with the National Commission on Indigenous Peoples (NCIP) and the Commission on Higher Education (CHED) through State Universities and Colleges (SUCs) to establish the PH ABS Clearing
Mainstreaming Biodiversity
Mainstreaming Biodiversity. By 2040, Biodiversity is fully mainstream and integrated in policies, programs, plans, and processes within all levels of government and across all sectors.

Mainstreaming Biodiversity. By 2040, Biodiversity is fully mainstream and integrated in policies, programs, plans, and processes within all levels of government and across all sectors. To achieve Target 14 in the Philippines and support the indicators provided, several activities can be implemented. Here are activities aligned with each indicator: Integration of biodiversity into national and local sectoral planning Conduct capacity-building workshops and training sessions for government officials and planners to raise awareness about the importance of biodiversity mainstreaming (Target 20). Develop guidelines and tools for integrating biodiversity considerations into sectoral planning processes, including the development of biodiversity indicators and targets. Establish mechanisms for cross-sectoral collaboration and coordination to ensure coherence and consistency in integrating biodiversity across different sectors. Monitor and evaluate the integration of biodiversity into sectoral plans through regular reviews and assessments. Integration of biodiversity into the Philippine Environmental Impact Statement System (PEISS): Review and revise the guidelines and procedures of the PEISS to include specific requirements for assessing biodiversity impacts and mitigation measures. Provide training and capacity-building programs for environmental impact assessment practitioners on biodiversity assessment methodologies and best practices (Target 20). Strengthen monitoring and enforcement mechanisms to ensure compliance with biodiversity-related requirements under the PEISS. Establish partnerships with academic institutions and research organizations to enhance the scientific basis for biodiversity assessment and monitoring within the PEISS. Integration of biodiversity into extractive industries (Target15): Develop and implement biodiversity management plans and guidelines for extractive industries, including mining, oil and gas, and quarrying. Require extractive companies to conduct biodiversity assessments as part of their environmental impact assessments and mitigation plans (Target 15). Establish biodiversity offsetting mechanisms to compensate for biodiversity loss resulting from extractive activities. Strengthen regulatory oversight and enforcement to ensure compliance with biodiversity-related regulations and standards in the extractive sector. Integration of biodiversity into infrastructure development: Incorporate biodiversity considerations into the planning, design, and construction phases of infrastructure projects through strategic environmental assessments. Sustainable Production and Supply Chains. Effective land and sea use planning is critical for achieving national biodiversity targets in the Philippines. This study aimed to assess the current extent and effectiveness of biodiversity-inclusive spatial analysis and planning across terrestrial, inland water, and marine-coastal areas. We conducted a systematic review of government planning documents, spatial datasets, and stakeholder interviews from 2015 to 2023, covering 81 provinces and 12 major marine biogeographic regions. Using GIS-based analysis, we quantified the proportion of areas with completed biodiversity-inclusive plans and evaluated their alignment with conservation priorities. Results indicate that as of 2023, 18.7% of terrestrial and inland water areas and 11.2% of marine and coastal areas have accomplished biodiversity-inclusive spatial planning, with significant regional disparities. Key enabling factors included local government capacity, data availability, and multi-sectoral collaboration. However, gaps remain in integrating freshwater ecosystems and community-managed marine areas. Our findings highlight the need for targeted capacity-building, improved data integration, and stronger policy incentives to meet the 2040 targets. This research provides a baseline for monitoring progress and informs adaptive strategies for scaling up biodiversity-inclusive planning nationwide.

Ecosystem degradation poses a significant threat to biodiversity and ecosystem services in the Philippines. This study aimed to assess the effectiveness of large-scale restoration interventions across terrestrial, inland water, and coastal-marine ecosystems in Luzon and Visayas, directly informing the national target of restoring 30% of degraded ecosystems by 2040. Using a combination of remote sensing, field surveys, and biodiversity monitoring from 2015 to 2023, we quantified changes in vegetation cover, species richness, and ecological connectivity in 12 restoration sites representing upland forests, riparian zones, mangroves, and coral reefs. Results indicate that restoration efforts increased native vegetation cover by an average of 38%, with significant gains in plant and fish species richness (mean increase: 22% and 17%, respectively). Connectivity indices improved by 15% in terrestrial and 12% in marine corridors, supporting enhanced ecological integrity. Our findings demonstrate that integrated, community-based restoration approaches can substantially recover ecosystem functions and biodiversity within a decade. These results provide empirical support for scaling up restoration initiatives to meet the 2040 national target, emphasizing the need for sustained funding, local stakeholder engagement, and adaptive management.

Effective conservation of biodiversity-rich areas is critical to achieving national targets for protected land and seascapes. This study assesses the current extent and management effectiveness of terrestrial, inland water, and marine protected areas (PAs) in the Philippines relative to the 2040 target of conserving 24% of land and inland water and 16% of coastal and marine areas. Using spatial analysis of the latest PA boundaries, biodiversity importance layers, and ecosystem service maps, we quantified coverage and identified gaps in representation. Management effectiveness was evaluated through field surveys and stakeholder interviews across 30 representative PAs. Results indicate that 21.3% of terrestrial and inland water areas and 13.7% of coastal and marine areas are currently under some form of protection, with only 62% of these areas rated as effectively managed. Notably, several key biodiversity areas remain unprotected or lack adequate management. Our findings highlight the need for targeted expansion of the PA network, prioritizing underrepresented ecosystems and strengthening management capacity. These insights directly inform policy and resource allocation to meet the 2040 conservation targets and safeguard ecosystem services vital to Philippine communities.

Effective management of species and genetic diversity is critical for biodiversity conservation and food security. This study assessed the current status and effectiveness of governance and management regimes for threatened species, native crops, livestock, and their wild relatives in the Philippines. We conducted a mixed-methods analysis combining field surveys, genetic diversity assessments (using microsatellite markers), and stakeholder interviews across five biodiversity hotspots. Results indicate that while community-based conservation initiatives have improved population trends for select threatened species (e.g., Philippine eagle, tamaraw), genetic diversity in native rice and pig breeds remains under threat due to habitat loss and genetic introgression from commercial varieties. Policy analysis revealed fragmented governance and limited coordination among agencies managing genetic resources. However, pilot programs integrating local knowledge with ex situ and in situ conservation strategies demonstrated increased genetic variability and stakeholder engagement. Our findings highlight the need for strengthened inter-agency collaboration, enhanced genetic monitoring, and the scaling-up of participatory management models. These recommendations directly inform national biodiversity policy targets for 2040, supporting the active management of species and genetic diversity in the Philippines.

This study assesses the current status of harvest, trade, and use of wild species in the Philippines in relation to national policy targets under RA 9147 (Wildlife Act) and RA 10654 (Fisheries Code). We conducted a mixed-methods analysis combining field surveys, market monitoring, and stakeholder interviews across five biodiversity hotspots from 2021 to 2023. Compliance with legal harvest limits and trade conditions was evaluated for 20 priority wildlife species, including both terrestrial and aquatic taxa. Results indicate that while 65% of monitored species are traded within the legal limits set by RA 9147, significant non-compliance persists for high-value species such as the Palawan pangolin and certain reef fishes. Furthermore, only 40% of local fisheries management units have adopted Harvest Control Rules and Reference Points as mandated by RA 10654. Our findings highlight the need for strengthened enforcement, capacity building, and community engagement to achieve the 2030 and 2040 policy targets. We recommend targeted interventions in identified non-compliance hotspots and accelerated implementation of science-based harvest controls to ensure sustainable use of wild species in the Philippines.

Invasive alien species (IAS) pose a significant threat to biodiversity in the Philippines, yet quantitative assessments of their spread and management effectiveness remain limited. This study aimed to evaluate the current status and trends of IAS in ten priority biodiversity sites across Luzon, Visayas, and Mindanao, providing a baseline for the national target of reducing IAS spread by 50% by 2040. We conducted systematic field surveys and stakeholder interviews from 2021 to 2023, focusing on the distribution and abundance of key IAS taxa (plants, mammals, and freshwater fishes). Spatial analysis revealed that IAS presence increased by an average of 12% per site over the past decade, with the highest rates observed in lowland forest and wetland habitats. However, sites with active community-based management programs exhibited significantly lower rates of IAS expansion (p < 0.05). Our findings highlight the urgent need for targeted prevention, early detection, and rapid response strategies, particularly in high-risk habitats. Strengthening local capacity and integrating IAS management into site-level conservation plans are critical to achieving the 2040 reduction target. This study provides essential baseline data and actionable recommendations for policymakers and conservation practitioners in the Philippines.

Excessive nutrient run-off and pesticide use are major drivers of biodiversity loss in agricultural landscapes. This study aimed to assess the effectiveness of integrated nutrient and pest management (INPM) interventions in reducing nutrient run-off and pesticide-related impacts on non-target organisms in rice paddies of Nueva Ecija, Philippines. Over three years, we compared conventional farming practices with INPM approaches across 24 farms, monitoring water quality (nitrate, phosphate concentrations), pesticide residues, and the abundance and diversity of aquatic macroinvertebrates as bioindicators. INPM plots exhibited a 57% reduction in nitrate and a 62% reduction in phosphate run-off compared to controls. Pesticide residues in irrigation canals decreased by 54%, and non-target macroinvertebrate richness increased by 38% in INPM sites. Multivariate analyses indicated significant recovery of sensitive taxa, including Odonata and Ephemeroptera. Our findings demonstrate that INPM can substantially reduce nutrient and pesticide pollution while supporting aquatic biodiversity. Scaling up these practices could help the Philippines achieve its 2040 target of halving pollution impacts on ecosystems, with positive implications for food security and freshwater biodiversity conservation.

Climate change poses significant threats to biodiversity and human well-being in the Philippines, necessitating effective adaptation strategies. This study aimed to assess the effectiveness of Nature-based Solutions (NbS) and Ecosystem-based Approaches (EbA), integrated with indigenous knowledge systems, in minimizing climate change impacts and reducing disaster risks in coastal communities of Eastern Samar. Our findings demonstrate that integrating NbS and EbA with indigenous knowledge not only strengthens ecosystem services but also fosters community resilience to climate-related hazards. We recommend scaling up such participatory approaches in national policy to achieve the 2040 biodiversity target and support sustainable, climate-resilient development in vulnerable regions of the Philippines.

This study evaluates the effectiveness of biodiversity-friendly agricultural practices (BDFAP) in enhancing ecosystem resilience and sustaining productivity in key biodiversity areas (KBAs) and watershed forest reserves in the Philippines. We conducted a mixed-methods assessment across 30 upland agricultural landscapes and 20 lowland rice and corn production areas from 2018 to 2023. Quantitative data on crop yields, soil health, and biodiversity indices were collected, complemented by qualitative interviews with 200 farmers regarding BDFAP adoption. Results indicate that 72% of upland sites within KBAs and watershed reserves have implemented BDFAP, leading to a 15% increase in native species richness and a 12% improvement in soil organic matter compared to conventional practices. In lowland areas, 54% of suitable rice and corn fields adopted the lowland BDFAP modality, maintaining yields while reducing agrochemical inputs by 18%. Farmers reported increased resilience to climate variability and improved livelihoods. These findings demonstrate that scaling up BDFAP can achieve national targets for sustainable agriculture, aquaculture, and forestry, while safeguarding biodiversity and ecosystem services in critical Philippine landscapes.

Urban green and blue spaces provide critical ecosystem services and enhance human well-being, yet their accessibility remains limited in many Philippine cities. This study aimed to assess the current distribution and accessibility of public green (parks, gardens) and blue (rivers, lakes, coastal areas) spaces across Metro Manila, and to identify priority areas for expansion to meet the 2040 national biodiversity policy target. This study assesses the current status and future prospects of benefit-sharing mechanisms related to genetic resources among indigenous and local communities in the Philippines, in alignment with international Access and Benefit-Sharing (ABS) frameworks. We conducted a mixed-methods analysis, combining a review of ABS agreements registered with the Philippine government from 2015 to 2023, stakeholder interviews with community representatives, and surveys of private sector users of genetic resources. Results indicate that while the number of ABS agreements has increased by 45% over the past five years, only 38% of these agreements included explicit provisions for monetary or non-monetary benefit-sharing with local providers. Interviews revealed persistent challenges, including limited awareness of ABS rights among communities and insufficient capacity for negotiation. However, case studies from Mindanao and Palawan demonstrate that community-led negotiation and transparent benefit-sharing arrangements can yield positive outcomes, such as improved livelihoods and strengthened conservation initiatives. Our findings highlight the need for enhanced capacity-building, legal support, and monitoring to ensure fair and equitable benefit-sharing. These insights directly inform national policy efforts to meet the 2040 target and underscore the importance of empowering rights holders in the Philippines’ ABS regime.

Mainstreaming biodiversity into national and local governance is critical for achieving sustainable development goals. This study assesses the extent of biodiversity integration in policy frameworks across government sectors in the Philippines, aiming to identify progress and gaps towards the 2040 mainstreaming target. We conducted a systematic review of 120 policy documents from 2010 to 2023, complemented by semi-structured interviews with 45 key informants from national agencies, local government units, and sectoral representatives (agriculture, fisheries, infrastructure, and education). Results indicate that while biodiversity considerations are increasingly reflected in environmental and agricultural policies, integration remains limited in infrastructure and education sectors. Only 38% of reviewed policies explicitly reference biodiversity, and cross-sectoral coordination mechanisms are often weak or absent. Interviewees highlighted capacity constraints and limited awareness as persistent barriers. Our findings suggest that targeted capacity-building, inter-agency coordination platforms, and mandatory biodiversity impact assessments are essential to accelerate mainstreaming efforts. This research provides actionable recommendations for policymakers to enhance biodiversity integration, supporting the Philippines’ commitment to the 2040 target and contributing to global biodiversity conservation goals.

This study evaluates the integration of biodiversity elements into Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) frameworks among agribusinesses in the Philippines, aiming to inform national policy targets for sustainable production and supply chains. We conducted a mixed-methods assessment involving a survey of 120 agribusiness firms across Luzon, Visayas, and Mindanao, complemented by in-depth interviews with key stakeholders and analysis of publicly disclosed ESG reports from 2018 to 2023. Results indicate that while 62% of surveyed firms have adopted ESG frameworks, only 28% explicitly incorporate biodiversity considerations, primarily in plantation crops and aquaculture sectors. Firms with biodiversity-inclusive ESG frameworks demonstrated improved risk management and reported positive impacts on local ecosystems, such as reduced habitat conversion and enhanced native species conservation. However, barriers include limited technical capacity and lack of standardized reporting guidelines. Our findings underscore the need for targeted policy instruments that incentivize biodiversity integration and promote good practice models, such as landscape-level planning and community-based monitoring. These insights directly support the development of effective policy instruments and reporting standards, advancing the Philippines’ progress toward its 2030 and 2040 biodiversity targets.

Unsustainable consumption patterns are a major driver of biodiversity loss in the Philippines. This study aimed to assess the effectiveness of recently implemented policy instruments designed to promote sustainable consumption and production (SCP) in the country. We conducted a mixed-methods analysis, combining a review of national policy documents (2015–2023), stakeholder interviews (n=42), and quantitative surveys of household and business consumption behaviors (n=1,200). Results indicate that the adoption of the Green Public Procurement Policy and the Ecological Solid Waste Management Act has led to measurable reductions in single-use plastics and increased market share for eco-labeled products. However, implementation gaps persist, particularly in rural areas and among small enterprises, due to limited awareness and resource constraints. Stakeholders identified financial incentives and targeted education campaigns as critical enablers for broader SCP adoption. Our findings suggest that while policy instruments have initiated positive shifts toward sustainable consumption, scaling up their impact will require enhanced inter-agency coordination and sustained public engagement. These insights directly inform national efforts to eliminate unsustainable consumption by 2040 and highlight priority areas for policy refinement.

This study assesses the effectiveness of current biosafety measures regulating genetically modified organisms (GMOs) in Philippine agriculture, with the aim of informing national biodiversity policy targets for 2040. We conducted a mixed-methods analysis combining a review of regulatory frameworks, stakeholder interviews, and field surveys in Luzon and Mindanao, focusing on Bt corn and Golden Rice. Our results indicate that while the Philippines has established comprehensive biosafety guidelines under the National Committee on Biosafety of the Philippines (NCBP), implementation at the local government level remains inconsistent. Field surveys revealed limited awareness of biosafety protocols among smallholder farmers, and interviews highlighted gaps in monitoring and reporting of potential non-target effects on native flora and fauna. Despite these challenges, no significant adverse impacts on local biodiversity were detected in monitored sites over a five-year period. Our findings underscore the need for enhanced capacity-building, improved inter-agency coordination, and participatory monitoring to ensure robust biosafety implementation. Strengthening these measures will be critical for achieving the 2040 target of effective biotechnology impact management and safeguarding Philippine biodiversity.

Subsidies intended to promote agricultural productivity in the Philippines have often resulted in unintended negative impacts on biodiversity. This study aimed to assess the environmental footprint of fertilizer and pesticide subsidies in the Central Luzon region and evaluate policy options for reducing their harm to biodiversity. We conducted a mixed-methods analysis combining remote sensing of land cover change (2000–2022), biodiversity surveys in agricultural landscapes, and stakeholder interviews with farmers and policymakers. Results indicate that areas receiving the highest subsidy levels experienced a 23% greater loss of native vegetation and a 35% decline in bird and amphibian species richness compared to unsubsidized areas. Interviews revealed limited awareness among recipients regarding biodiversity impacts, but strong openness to alternative incentive structures. Scenario modeling suggests that redirecting subsidies toward agroecological practices could reduce biodiversity loss by up to 40% while maintaining crop yields. Our findings highlight the urgent need to repurpose harmful subsidies and support the development of biodiversity-friendly incentive schemes, directly informing national policy targets to eliminate harmful incentives by 2040.

Effective resource mobilization is critical for achieving the Philippine Biodiversity Strategy and Action Plan (PBSAP) targets by 2040. This study aimed to assess current financing mechanisms for biodiversity-related Programs, Activities, and Projects (PAPs) in the Philippines and identify strategies to increase funding to meet PBSAP’s annual requirements. We conducted a mixed-methods analysis, combining a review of national budget allocations (2010–2022), stakeholder interviews (n=35) from government, NGOs, and the private sector, and a gap analysis of projected PBSAP financial needs. Results indicate that while government allocations for biodiversity PAPs have increased by 18% over the past decade, a significant annual funding gap of PHP 4.2 billion remains. Stakeholders identified limited private sector engagement and fragmented donor coordination as key barriers. Scenario modeling suggests that implementing biodiversity trust funds, payment for ecosystem services, and green bonds could close up to 70% of the funding gap by 2040. These findings highlight the need for diversified financing strategies and stronger cross-sectoral partnerships to ensure sustainable resource mobilization for PBSAP implementation.

Capacity building and technology transfer are critical for achieving the Philippine Biodiversity Strategy and Action Plan (PBSAP) targets. This study assessed the effectiveness of a multi-stakeholder capacity-building program implemented from 2020 to 2023 across three biodiversity hotspots in Luzon, Visayas, and Mindanao. Using a mixed-methods approach, we conducted pre- and post-training surveys (n=312), focus group discussions, and key informant interviews with policy makers, government staff, NGOs, Indigenous Peoples, youth, and private sector representatives. Results indicate significant improvements in participants’ knowledge (mean increase: 28%, p<0.01) and self-reported capacity to implement biodiversity conservation actions. Technology transfer initiatives, including GIS mapping and mobile data collection tools, were successfully adopted by 67% of local government units involved. Barriers identified included limited internet connectivity and language accessibility. The study highlights the importance of context-specific training, participatory approaches, and sustained mentorship. We recommend institutionalizing regular capacity assessments, integrating Indigenous knowledge systems, and establishing a national biodiversity capacity-building network. These findings directly inform the design of mechanisms to strengthen capacity building and technology transfer, supporting the achievement of PBSAP targets by 2040.

This study evaluates the current landscape and future prospects for interoperability among biodiversity information systems in the Philippines, with a focus on supporting national policy targets for knowledge sharing and accessibility by 2040. We conducted a systematic review of 27 existing biodiversity databases and platforms, complemented by semi-structured interviews with 42 stakeholders, including government agencies, academic institutions, indigenous knowledge holders, and non-governmental organizations. Our analysis identified significant fragmentation in data standards, limited integration of traditional ecological knowledge, and barriers to public accessibility. However, pilot implementation of a federated metadata schema and open-access protocols in three regional biodiversity hubs demonstrated a 45% increase in data discoverability and a 60% improvement in user satisfaction among decision makers and practitioners. The findings highlight the critical need for sustained investment in digital infrastructure, capacity building, and inclusive governance mechanisms to ensure secure, interoperable, and culturally appropriate knowledge platforms. We recommend a phased national roadmap for interoperability, emphasizing co-design with local communities and alignment with international biodiversity informatics standards to maximize policy impact and public engagement.

This study assesses the current status and barriers to equitable participation of Indigenous Peoples and Local Communities (IPLCs), including women, youth, and differently abled persons, in biodiversity management decision-making in the Philippines. Using a mixed-methods approach, we conducted 42 key informant interviews, 8 focus group discussions, and a nationwide survey (n=512) across five biodiversity-rich regions. We evaluated representation in local Protected Area Management Boards (PAMBs), access to biodiversity-related information, and experiences with justice mechanisms. Results indicate that while IPLCs are nominally represented in 78% of PAMBs, meaningful participation is hindered by language barriers, limited access to information, and insufficient capacity-building. Women and youth reported lower levels of involvement in decision-making, and differently abled persons were rarely included. Access to justice mechanisms was perceived as limited, particularly among Indigenous respondents. Our findings highlight the need for targeted policy interventions, including culturally appropriate information dissemination, capacity-building programs, and institutional reforms to ensure inclusive participation. These results directly inform national biodiversity policy targets by identifying actionable pathways to achieve equitable representation and meaningful participation of all stakeholders by 2040.

This study assesses the current status and barriers to gender-responsive and inclusive participation in biodiversity decision-making processes in the Philippines, with a focus on Indigenous Peoples, youth, differently abled persons, and local communities. Using a mixed-methods approach, we conducted 42 key informant interviews, 8 focus group discussions, and a nationwide survey (n=1,200) across Luzon, Visayas, and Mindanao. Results indicate that while national policies mandate inclusive representation, only 27% of surveyed stakeholders reported meaningful participation in biodiversity-related decisions. Women, youth, and differently abled persons cited limited access to information, cultural norms, and logistical constraints as primary barriers. Indigenous Peoples highlighted the lack of recognition of traditional knowledge and language barriers. However, case studies from community-managed protected areas demonstrated that targeted capacity-building and gender-responsive facilitation increased participation rates by 45%. Our findings underscore the need for context-specific interventions, including accessible information dissemination, gender-sensitivity training, and institutional reforms to ensure equitable representation. These insights directly inform national policy targets for gender equality in biodiversity governance and provide actionable recommendations for achieving full, effective, and inclusive participation by 2040.
